manuscript.title: Whale Optimization Algorithm and Moth-Flame Optimization for Multilevel Thresholding Image Segmentation
manuscript.abstract_text: Determining the optimal thresholding for image segmentation has got more attention in re- cent years since it has many applications. There are several methods used to ﬁnd the optimal thresholding values such as Otsu and Kapur based methods. These methods are suitable for bi-level thresholding case and they can be easily extended to the multilevel case, however, the process of determining the optimal thresholds in the case of multilevel thresholding is time- consuming. To avoid this problem, this paper examines the ability of two nature inspired algorithms namely: Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) and Moth-Flame Optimization (MFO) to determine the optimal multilevel thresholding for image segmentation. The MFO algorithm is inspired from the natural behavior of moths which have a special navigation style at night since they ﬂy using the moonlight, whereas, the WOA algorithm emulates the natural cooperative behaviors of whales. The candidate solutions in the adapted algorithms were created using the image histogram, and then they were updated based on the character- istics of each algorithm. The solutions are assessed using the Otsu’s ﬁtness function during the optimization operation. The performance of the proposed algorithms has been evaluated using several of benchmark images and has been compared with ﬁve diﬀerent swarm algo- rithms. The results have been analyzed based on the best ﬁtness values, PSNR, and SSIM measures, as well as time complexity and the ANOVA test. The experimental results showed that the proposed methods outperformed the other swarm algorithms; in addition, the MFO showed better results than WOA, as well as provided a good balance between exploration and exploitation in all images at small and high threshold numbers.

sections.heading_text: The Proposed Algorithms for Multilevel Thresholding
sections.body_text: In this section, we introduce two algorithms that will be used to determine the optimal multilevel thresholding for image segmentation that maximizes the Otsu’s objective function.

The Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) was proposed by the authors of (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016) inspired from the behavior of the humpback whales. For the multilevel thresholding problem, the goal of the WOA algorithm is to determine the position in the search space (the optimal threshold values) that optimizes the considered objective function given by Equation (2). The input to this algorithm is the image histogram and the output is the optimal position ⃗X∗that represents the optimal threshold. Each indi- vidual whale ⃗Xi(i = 1, ..., N) is represented as a vector of possible real values corresponding to thresholds as follows (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016): ⃗Xi = (xi,1, xi,2, ..., xi,K)T, subject to 0 < xi,1... < xi,K < L (6) where xi,1 corresponding to t1 in Equation (2). The position of each individual whale of the population is generated randomly in the range [gmin, gmax], where gmin and gmax are the minimum and the maximum gray levels in the image histogram, respectively. This can be expressed by the following equation (Mirjalili & Lewis, 2016): xi,j = gmin + rand(0, 1) × (gmax −gmin), xi,j ∈⃗Xi, j = (1, 2, ..., K) (7) Then the ﬁtness function for each whale is computed and the best ﬁtness function Fg is determined and its corresponding position is ⃗X∗.

The authors of (Mirjalili, 2015) modeled the natural behavior of moths in a mathematical form to provide the MFO algorithm as a new metaheuristic algorithm. In this paper, the MFO algorithm has been applied to determine the multilevel thresholding as follows; a population of N individual moth is created. Each individual moth or solution ⃗Xi (i = 1, ..., N) is encoded as shown in Equation (6). Each ⃗Xi uses K decision variables that each one represents a diﬀerent threshold point xi,j(j = 1, ..., K) that is used for the multilevel image thresholding. The position of each individual moth in the population is initialized using Equation (7) and evaluated using Equation (2), then the optimal position of moths is saved in flames. In this section, we introduce the environment of the experiments for the proposed al- gorithms. The description of benchmark images is introduced ﬁrstly, then the parameters setting for each algorithm are illustrated brieﬂy and a set of quality metrics are used to evaluate the quality of the segmentation process.

In this paper, the proposed algorithms are tested on eight common grayscale images from the database of Berkeley University (Martin et al., 2001). These images are called, TestE4, TestE1, Test1, Test6, Test5, Test11, Test3, and Test9 as illustrated in Figure 3.

The results of the proposed algorithms are compared with other ﬁve evolutionary algo- rithms, namely, SCA (Mirjalili, 2016), HS (Oliva et al., 2013), SSO (Ouadfel & Taleb-Ahmed, 2016), FASSO (Abd El-Aziz et al., 2016), and FA; these algorithms were applied in previous works and proved good results. The results of the proposed algorithms compared to other algorithms are illustrated in Tables 2-6 and Figures 4-7. Tables 2 and 3 show the ﬁtness values and the optimal threshold values obtained by the algorithms over 30 runs, respectively. The results in Table 2 and Figure 4 indicate that all the algorithms performed nearly equally whenever K = 2, however, the WOA algorithm is the highest ﬁtness function and the FA algorithm comes at the second rank followed by MFO. When K = 3, the SSO, FA and FASSO have nearly the same ﬁtness function, however, the WOA and MFO are better than the rest algorithms. A parametric statistical test known as ”the analysis of variance” (ANOVA) test has been conducted with a 5% signiﬁcance level to test the signiﬁcant diﬀerence between algorithms. In the experiments, the proposed algorithms were chosen as the control group and were com- pared with the SCA, HS, FASSO and FA algorithms in terms of the mean value of the four measures (which are normally distributed). The null hypothesis assumes that there is no sig- niﬁcant diﬀerence between the mean values of the four algorithms; whereas, the alternative hypothesis considers a signiﬁcant diﬀerence between them. Table 7 reports, the p −value was produced by the ANOVA test for the ﬁtness function, execution time, SSIM and PSNR measures (Note: the (*) indicates that there exists a signif- icant diﬀerence). Based on the ﬁtness function, the p −value is greater than 0.05, therefore, the null hypothesis is accepted and this indicates that there is no diﬀerence between the proposed algorithms and the other algorithms. However, the MFO has the highest ﬁtness function, and the WOA is better than all other algorithms except SSO and FASSO. The p −value for SSIM, PSNR, and execution time is less than 0.05, therefore, we accept the alternative hypothesis that refers to a signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the proposed algo- rithms and other algorithms. In general, there are existent signiﬁcant diﬀerences between the proposed algorithms and both of SCA and HS in terms of all measures. In this paper, the problem of determining the optimal thresholding in a case of multilevel thresholding for image segmentation has been considered as an optimization problem where the Otsu’s method has been used as a ﬁtness function. Therefore, two new swarm algorithms, namely, the WOA and MFO have been proposed to solve this problem. The aim of each algorithm is to determine the best thresholds value that maximizes the Otsu’s function. The experimental results of the proposed algorithms have been compared to SCA, HS, SSO, FASSO, and FA algorithms. The performance of each algorithm has been assessed based on four measures, the best ﬁtness values, PSNR, SSIM, and execution time. We used eight benchmark images in all experiments. The obtained results showed that all the algorithms achieved the same ﬁtness function value at a threshold level equal two; this is because the segmentation problem becomes easy at this level of threshold. At the three-level thresholding, the WOA and MFO algorithms are better than other algorithms on almost all images, in terms of PSNR and SSIM, however, WOA is better than MFO. For a higher number of thresholds, the MFO algorithm is better than WOA algorithm in all images, and in terms of the ﬁtness value, PSNR, and SSIM.
